page.title: Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565

revision.text:
{{Short description|Organ music by Johann Sebastian Bach}} {{Redirect|Toccata and Fugue in D minor|the Toccata and Fugue in D minor known as "Dorian"|Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 538}} [[File:Ringk Copy - First Page Fragment.jpg|upright=1.3|thumb|Beginning of BWV 565 in [[Johannes Ringk]]'s manuscript, which is, as far as known, the only extant 18th-century copy of the work]] {{listen|type=music|filename=Toccata et Fugue BWV565.ogg|title=Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565|description=Performed by Ashtar Moïra on organ}} The '''Toccata and Fugue in D minor''', [[Bach-Werke-Verzeichnis|BWV]] 565, is a composition for [[Pipe organ|organ]] from the [[Baroque music|Baroque]] period which was long attributed to [[Johann Sebastian Bach]], but whose authorship has been questioned by a minority of scholars since 1981. It is one of the most widely recognisable works in the [[organ repertoire]].{{sfn|Billeter|2004|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=uPZ0Kv2Ez1gC&pg=PA159 159]}} It was written between 1704 and the 1750s.{{sfn|Williams|2003}} The piece opens with a [[toccata]] section followed by a [[fugue]] that ends in a [[coda (music)|coda]], and is typical of the [[north German organ school]] of the Baroque era.
Little was known about its early existence until the piece was discovered in an undated manuscript produced by [[Johannes Ringk]]. It was first published in 1833 during the early [[Bach Revival]] period through the efforts of composer [[Felix Mendelssohn]], who also performed the piece in 1840. In the 20th century, its popularity rose above that of other organ compositions by Bach, as exemplified by its inclusion in [[Walt Disney]]'s 1940 animated film ''[[Fantasia (1940 film)|Fantasia]]'' using [[Leopold Stokowski]]'s orchestral transcription from 1927.
The piece has been subject to a wide, and often conflicting, variety of analyses. It is often described as a type of [[program music]] depicting a storm, while its depiction in ''Fantasia'' is suggestive of non-representational or [[absolute music]].
The English musicologist [[Peter Williams (musicologist)|Peter Williams]] questioned its authorship in 1981. The musicologist [[Christoph Wolff|Christoph Wolff]], the world's foremost living Bach scholar, believes that the piece is by Bach.
==History== The only extant near-contemporary source for BWV 565 is an undated copy by [[Johannes Ringk]].<ref name="Zehnder2011commp5">[[#Zehnder 2011 (score)|Zehnder 2011 (score)]], [https://www.breitkopf.com/bach-edirom/apps/breitkopf-bach-band-4/EB_8804.pdf "Commentary"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210503154553/https://www.breitkopf.com/bach-edirom/apps/breitkopf-bach-band-4/EB_8804.pdf |date=2021-05-03 }} pp. 4–5</ref>{{sfn|Claus|2000}} According to the description provided by the [[Berlin State Library]], where the manuscript is kept, and similar bibliographic descriptions, e.g. in the [[Répertoire International des Sources Musicales|RISM]] catalogue, Ringk created his copy between 1740 and 1760.<ref name="Ringk">[[#Ringk (score)|Ringk (score)]]</ref><ref>{{RISM|467300997}}. {{Retrieved|access-date=6 November 2020}}</ref> As far as is known, Ringk produced his first copy of a Bach score in 1730 when he was 12.<ref name="Zehnder2011commp5" />{{sfn|Billeter|2004|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=uPZ0Kv2Ez1gC&pg=PA160 160]}} According to [[Dietrich Kilian]], who edited BWV 565 for the [[New Bach Edition]], Ringk made his copy of the Toccata and Fugue between 1730 and 1740.{{sfn|Billeter|2004|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=uPZ0Kv2Ez1gC&pg=PA160 160]}} In his critical commentary for [[Breitkopf & Härtel]]'s 21st-century revised edition of the score, [[Jean-Claude Zehnder]] narrows the time of origin of the manuscript down to around the middle of the first half of the 1730s, based on an analysis of the evolution of Ringk's handwriting.<ref name="Zehnder2011commp5" /> At the time Ringk was a student of Bach's former student{{sfn|Billeter|2004}} [[Johann Peter Kellner]] at [[Gräfenroda]], and probably faithfully copied what his teacher put before him.<ref name="Zehnder2011commp5" /> There are some errors in the score such as note values not adding up to fill a measure correctly. Such defects show a carelessness deemed typical of Kellner, who left over 60 copies of works by Bach.<ref name="Zehnder2011commp5" /><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bach-digital.de/receive/BachDigitalPerson_agent_00003065?lang=en |title=Kellner, Johann Peter |date=2020-06-19 |website=[[Bach Digital]] |publisher=[[Bach Archive]]; et al. |location=Leipzig |access-date=2020-11-08 |archive-date=2021-09-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210928174952/https://www.bach-digital.de/receive/BachDigitalPerson_agent_00003065?lang=en |url-status=live }}</ref>
The title page of Ringk's manuscript writes the title of the work in Italian as ''Toccata con Fuga'', names Johann Sebastian Bach as the composer of the piece, and indicates its [[tonality]] as "ex. d. #.", which is usually seen as the [[key signature]] being [[D minor]]. However, in Ringk's manuscript the staves have no {{flat}} symbol at the key (which would later become the standard way to write down a piece in D minor). Most modern score editions of BWV 565 use the D minor key signature, unlike Ringk's manuscript.<ref name="Ringk" /><ref name="Kilian1964pVI">[[#Kilian 1964 (score)|Kilian 1964 (score)]], p. vi</ref> Another piece listed as Bach's was also known as Toccata and Fugue in D minor, which received the "Dorian" nickname, that qualifier being effectively used to distinguish it from BWV 565.
{{gallery |title=Ringk manuscript |width=360 | height=470 | align=center | noborder=yes |footer={{big|Digital facsimiles of the Ringk manuscript became widely available in the 21st century.}} |File:Rincgk 01.jpg |[[:File:Rincgk 01.jpg|Title page]] |File:Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 (Johannes Ringk manuscript).jpg |[[:File:Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 (Johannes Ringk manuscript).jpg|pg 1]] }} {{gallery |width=160 | height=170 | align=center | noborder=yes |File:Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 (Johannes Ringk manuscript, pg2).jpg |[[:File:Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 (Johannes Ringk manuscript, pg2).jpg|pg 2]] |File:Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 (Johannes Ringk manuscript, pg3).jpg |[[:File:Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 (Johannes Ringk manuscript, pg3).jpg|pg 3]] |File:Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 (Johannes Ringk manuscript, pg4).jpg |[[:File:Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 (Johannes Ringk manuscript, pg4).jpg|pg 4]] |File:Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 (Johannes Ringk manuscript, pg5).jpg |[[:File:Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 (Johannes Ringk manuscript, pg5).jpg|pg 5]] |File:Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 (Johannes Ringk manuscript, pg6of6).jpg |[[:File:Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 (Johannes Ringk manuscript, pg6of6).jpg|pg 6]] }}
Ringk's manuscript does not use a separate staff for the pedal part, which was common in the 18th century (notes to be played on the pedal were indicated by "p." being written at the start of the sequence). Printed editions of the BWV 565 organ score invariably write the pedal line on a separate staff. In Ringk's manuscript the upper staff is written down using the [[soprano clef]] (as was common in the time when the manuscript originated), where printed editions use the [[treble clef]].<ref name="Ringk" /><ref name="Kilian1964pVI" /> [[File:T&F opening.gif|thumb|left|upright=2.6|Beginning, Ringk's "Dorian" notation – layout like Ringk's manuscript apart from position of [[fermata]]s and the clef for the upper staff]] [[File:D Dorian mode.png|thumb|upright=1.3|"D Dorian" mode notation used by Ringk for BWV 565]]{{clear}} All other extant manuscript copies of the score date from at least several decades later: some of these, written in the 19th century, are related with each other in that they have similar solutions to the defects in the Ringk manuscript. Whether these derive from an earlier manuscript independent from Ringk's (possibly in the [[C. P. E. Bach]]/[[Johann Friedrich Agricola]]/[[Johann Kirnberger]] circle) is debated by scholars. These near-identical 19th-century copies, the version [[Felix Mendelssohn]] knew, use the treble clef and a separate staff for the pedal. In general, the later copies show a less extensive use of fermatas in the opening measures and have fewer measures that do not add up properly, but that may as well be from polishing a defective source as from deriving from a cleaner earlier source. In the later copies the work is named for instance "Adagio" and "Fuga" (for the respective parts of the work), or "Toccata" for the work as a whole.<ref name="Zehnder2011commp5" />{{sfn|Williams|2003}} [[File:Bach Toccata d-moll BWV 565 begin.jpg|thumb|left|upright=2.6|Beginning, D minor notation, with the pedal part on a separate staff (also, [[arpeggio]] in second half of second measure converted to modern notation)]] [[File:D natural minor scale ascending and descending.png|thumb|upright=1.3|D minor: usual notation with a {{flat}} at the key]]{{clear}} The name "Toccata" is most probably a later addition, similar to the title of [[Toccata, Adagio and Fugue in C major, BWV 564|Toccata, Adagio and Fugue]], BWV 564, because in the Baroque era such organ pieces would most commonly be called simply ''Prelude'' (''Praeludium'', etc.) or ''Prelude and Fugue''.<ref name="Williams1981p331">Williams 1981, p. 331</ref> Ringk's copy abounds in Italian ''[[tempo]]'' markings, fermatas (a characteristic feature of Ringk's copies) and [[staccato]] dots, all very unusual features for pre-1740 German music.{{sfn|Williams|2003}}
[[German organ schools]] are distinguished into north German (e.g. [[Dieterich Buxtehude]]) and south German (e.g. [[Johann Pachelbel]]). The composition has stylistic characteristics from both schools: the [[stylus phantasticus]],<ref>[[Friedhelm Krummacher|Krummacher, Friedhelm]]. "Bach's Free Organ Works and the 'stylus Phantasticus{{'"}}, pp. 157–171, in {{harvnb|Stauffer|May|1986}}</ref> and other north German characteristics are most apparent.<ref name="Spitta1873p402">Spitta 1873, [https://books.google.com/books?id=HxkDAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA402 Vol. I pp. 402–403]</ref><ref name="Spitta1899p403">Spitta 1899, [https://archive.org/stream/johannsebastianb01spituoft#page/403/mode/1up Vol. I pp. 403–404]</ref> However, the numerous [[recitative]] stretches are rarely found in the works of northern composers and may have been inspired by [[Johann Heinrich Buttstett]],{{sfn|Williams|2003}} a pupil of Pachelbel, whose few surviving free works, particularly his Prelude and Capriccio in D minor, exhibit similar features. A passage in the fugue of BWV 565 is an exact copy of a phrase in one of Johann Pachelbel's D minor fantasias, and the first half of the subject is based on this Pachelbel passage as well. At the time it was however common practice to create fugues on other composers' themes.<ref name="newman181">Newman 1995, 181.</ref>
==Structure== BWV 565 exhibits a typical simplified [[German organ schools|north German]] structure with a short, free opening ([[toccata]]), a longer fugal section ([[fugue]]), and a short free closing section which is not officially named by notation.{{sfn|Williams|2003}}
===Toccata=== The Toccata begins with a single-voice flourish in the upper ranges of the keyboard, doubled at the [[octave]] and ornamented with a lower [[mordent]]. It then spirals toward the bottom, where a [[diminished seventh chord]] appears (which actually implies a [[Dominant (music)|dominant]] chord with a minor 9th against a [[Tonic (music)|tonic]] pedal), built one note at a time. This resolves into a D major chord:{{sfn|Williams|2003}} {| |- | {{Block indent|<score> \new Score << \new PianoStaff << \new Staff \with { \magnifyStaff #3/4 } << \new Voice \relative c''' { \set PianoStaff.connectArpeggios = ##t \override Score.NonMusicalPaperColumn #'line-break-permission = ##f \tempo Adagio \voiceOne a8 \fermata \mordent b,32 \rest g'64 f e d cis32 d16 b \rest b8 \rest \fermata a \fermata \mordent b32 \rest e, f cis d16 b' \rest b8 \rest \fermata | s2. \oneVoice <bes, cis e>4 ~ \arpeggio <bes cis e>4 d } \new Voice \relative c'' { \voiceTwo a8 \fermata \mordent s32 g64 f e d cis32 d16 s8. s2 | s1 s4 a } >> \new Staff \with { \magnifyStaff #3/4 } << \new Voice \relative c' { \clef "bass" s2 a8 \fermata \mordent d,32 \rest e f cis d16 d \rest d8 \rest \fermata | \voiceOne a'8 \fermata \mordent d,32 \rest g64 f e d cis32 d16 d16 \rest d8 \rest \fermata d4 \rest <cis e g>4 ~ \arpeggio | <cis e g> ~ g'16 e fis8 } \new Voice \relative c { \voiceTwo s1 a8 \fermata \mordent s32 g64 f e d cis32 d16 s8. s2 | s4 d'4 } >> >> \new Staff \with { \magnifyStaff #3/4 } \relative c, { \clef "bass" R1 | r2 d ~ | d } >> </score>}} | {{listen|type=music|filename=BWV-565-intro.ogg|title=Opening of the toccata|description=played on the Flentrop organ at the [[Oberlin Conservatory of Music]]|style=float:left|help=no|plain=yes}} |} Three short passages follow, each reiterating a short motif and doubled at the octave. The section ends with a diminished seventh chord which resolved into the [[Tonic (music)|tonic]], D minor, through a flourish. The second section of the Toccata is a number of loosely connected figurations and flourishes; the pedal switches to the [[Dominant (music)|dominant]] key, A minor. This section segues into the third and final section of the Toccata, which consists almost entirely of a passage doubled at the [[Interval (music)|sixth]] and comprising reiterations of the same three-note figure, similar to doubled passages in the first section. After a brief pedal flourish, the piece ends with a D minor suspended chord which eventually resolves.{{sfn|Williams|2003}}
===Fugue=== The subject of the four-voice [[fugue]] is made up entirely of [[sixteenth note]]s, with an implied [[pedal point]] set against a brief melodic subject that first falls, then rises. Such violinistic figures are frequently encountered in Baroque music and that of Bach, both as fugue subjects and as material in non-imitative pieces. Unusually, the answer is in the [[subdominant]] key, rather than the traditional dominant. Although technically a four-part fugue, most of the time there are only three voices, and some of the interludes are in two, or even one voice (notated as two). Although only simple triadic harmony is employed throughout the fugue, there is an unexpected C minor subject entry, and furthermore, a solo pedal statement of the subject—a unique feature for a Baroque fugue.<ref name="Yearsley 2012, 93">Yearsley 2012, p. 93</ref> Immediately after the final subject entry, the fugue resolves to a sustained B{{music|flat}} major chord.{{sfn|Williams|2003}}<ref name="newman181" />
===Coda=== A multi-sectional [[Coda (music)|coda]] follows, marked ''Recitativo''. Although only 17 bars long, it progresses through five tempo changes. The last bars are played ''Molto adagio'', and the piece ends with a minor [[Cadence (music)#Plagal cadence|plagal cadence]].{{sfn|Williams|2003}}
==Performance== The performance time of the piece is usually around nine minutes, but shorter performance times (e.g., 8:15<ref>Alain 1982 (recording)</ref> or 7:59<ref>Chapuis 1967 (recording)</ref>) and execution times of over 10:30<ref name="Schweitzer1951">Schweitzer 1951 (recording)</ref> exist. The first section of the piece, the Toccata, takes somewhat less than a third of the total performance time.<ref>Biggs 1960 (recording)</ref><ref name="Walcha1963">Walcha 1963 (recording)</ref>
As was common practice for German music of the 17th century, the intended [[Registration (organ)|registration]] is not specified, and performers' choices vary from simple solutions such as ''organo pleno'' to exceedingly complex ones, like those described by [[Harvey Grace]].<ref name="Grace1922p60">Grace 1922, [https://archive.org/stream/organworksofbach00grac#page/60/mode/2up pp. 60–65]</ref>
==Reception== In the first century of its existence the entire reception history of the Toccata and Fugue in D minor consists of being saved from oblivion by maybe not more than a single manuscript copy.<ref name="Zehnder2011p20">[[#Zehnder 2011 (score)|Zehnder 2011 (score)]], Introduction, p. 20</ref> Then it took about a century from its first publication as a little-known organ composition by Johann Sebastian Bach to becoming one of the signature pieces of the composer. The composition's third century took it from Bach's most often recorded organ piece to a composition with an unclear origin. Despite Mendelssohn's opinion that it was "at the same time learned and something for the people",<ref>Stinson 2006, [https://archive.org/details/receptionofbachs00stin/page/18 pp. 18–19]</ref> followed by a fairly successful piano transcription in the second half of the 19th century,<ref>[http://onyxclassics.com/sleevenotes.php?ID=158 Joseph Moog – Scarlatti Illuminated] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304081456/http://onyxclassics.com/sleevenotes.php?ID=158 |date=2016-03-04 }} at {{URL|onyxclassics.com}}</ref> it was not until the 20th century that it rose above the average notability of an organ piece by Bach.<ref name="Zehnder2011p20" /><ref name="Smith 2004">Rollin Smith. [https://books.google.com/books?id=t2fnSauvNsEC ''Stokowski and the Organ''.] Pendragon Press, 2004 {{ISBN|978-1576471036}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=t2fnSauvNsEC&pg=PA161 pp. 161 ff.]</ref> The work's appearance (in an orchestral transcription by [[Leopold Stokowski]]) in the 1940 Walt Disney film ''[[Fantasia (1940 film)|Fantasia]]'' contributed to its popularity,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Crist |first1=Stephen A. |editor1-last=Butt |editor1-first=John |title=The Cambridge Companion to Bach |date=1997 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0521587808 |page=75 |url=https://doi.org/10.1017/CCOL9780521587808.008 |chapter=The early works and the heritage of the seventeenth century |doi=10.1017/CCOL9780521587808.008 |access-date=2021-09-25 |archive-date=2021-09-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210928174955/https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cambridge-companion-to-bach/early-works-and-the-heritage-of-the-seventeenth-century/233EBEF2B3938EE38E25F5605C037BFC |url-status=live }}</ref> around which time scholars started to seriously doubt its attribution to Bach.<ref name="Williams1981">Williams 1981</ref>
The composition has been deemed both "particularly suited to the organ"<ref name="Spitta1899p403" /> and "strikingly unorganistic".<ref name="Fagius1988liner">Liner notes of Fagius 1988 (recording)</ref> It has been seen as united by a single ground-thought,<ref name="Schweitzer1935" /> but also as containing "passages which have no connection whatever with the chief idea".<ref name="Spitta1899p403" /> It has been called "entirely a thing of virtuosity"<ref name="Pirro1902p35">Pirro 1902, [https://archive.org/stream/johannsebastian00goodgoog#page/n65/mode/1up p. 35]</ref> yet also described as being "not so difficult as it sounds".<ref name="Grace1922p60" /> It has been described as some sort of [[program music]] depicting a storm,<ref name="Pirro1902p35" /> and, contrarily, as abstract music.<ref>Theodore Gracyk (2013). [https://books.google.com/books?id=_1hblGP-FAYC&pg=PA39 ''On Music'', pp. 39–40.] Routledge. {{ISBN|978-1136506567}}</ref> It has been presented as an emanation of the [[galant music|galant style]], yet too dramatic to be anything near that style.<ref name="Zehnder2011p20" /> Its period of origin has been assumed to have been as early as around 1704,{{sfn|Stauffer|1978}} and as late as the 1750s.{{sfn|Williams|2003}} Its defining characteristics have been associated with extant compositions by Bach ([[List of compositions by Johann Sebastian Bach#BWV531|BWV 531]], [[List of compositions by Johann Sebastian Bach#BWV531|549a]], [[BWV 578|578]], [[BWV 911|911]], [[BWV 914|914]], [[BWV 922|922]] and several of the [[sonatas and partitas for solo violin (Bach)|solo violin sonatas and partitas]]),{{sfn|Williams|2003}}<ref name="Spitta1899p403" /><ref name="Marshall2003">Marshall, Robert Lewis (2003). [https://books.google.com/books?id=skiY9f58hcIC&pg=PA61 "Johann Sebastian Bach" pp. 61 ff.] in ''Eighteenth-Century Keyboard Music'', edited by Robert Lewis Marshall. Psychology Press. {{ISBN|978-0415966429}}</ref><ref name="Spitta1899p434">Spitta 1899, [https://archive.org/stream/johannsebastianb01spituoft#page/434/mode/2up Vol. I pp. 434–435]</ref><ref name="Argent2000">{{harvnb|Argent|2000}}</ref> and by others (including [[Nicolaus Bruhns]] and [[Johann Heinrich Buttstett]]),{{sfn|Williams|2003}} as well as with untraceable earlier versions for other instruments and/or by other composers.{{sfn|Williams|2003}} It has been deemed too simplistic for it to have been written down by Bach,{{sfn|Williams|2003}} and too much a stroke of genius to have been composed by anyone but Bach.<ref name="Keller1948p64">Keller 1948, pp. 64 ff.</ref>
What remains is "the most famous organ work in existence",<ref name="Kranenburg2010">Kranenburg 2010, p. 88</ref> that in its rise to fame was helped by various arrangements, including bombastic piano settings,<ref>Stinson 2006, [https://books.google.com/books?id=0u5xOkBJpMEC&pg=PA120 p. 120]</ref> versions for full symphonic orchestra,<ref name="Stokowski 1927 recording">Stokowski 1927 (recording)</ref> and alternative settings for more modest solo instruments.{{sfn|Williams|2003}}
===Score editions=== In 1833, BWV 565 was published for the first time, in the third of three bundles of "little-known" organ compositions by Bach.<ref name="Marx1833">Marx, Adolf Bernhard (1795–1866), 1833 (score) (can't find this print source on OPAC-RISM catalog)</ref> The edition was conceived and partly prepared by [[Felix Mendelssohn]], who already had BWV 565 in his repertoire by 1830.<ref>Stinson 2006, [https://archive.org/details/receptionofbachs00stin/page/31 pp. 31–32]</ref> In 1846, [[C. F. Peters]] published the ''Toccata con Fuga'' as No. 4 in their fourth volume of organ compositions by Bach.<ref>Griepenkerl and Roitzsch 1846 (score)</ref> In 1867, the [[Bach Gesellschaft]] included it in Band 15 of its complete edition of Bach's works.<ref>Rust 1867 (score)</ref> [[Novello & Co|Novello]] published the work in 1886 as No. 1 in their sixth volume of Bach's organ works.<ref>Bridge 1886 (score)</ref>
In the early 1910s, [[Albert Schweitzer]] collaborated with [[Charles-Marie Widor]] to compile a complete edition of Bach's organ compositions, published by [[G. Schirmer Inc.|Schirmer]].<ref>Schweitzer 1995</ref> In 1912, BWV 565 was published in the second volume, containing works of Bach's "first master period".<ref>Widor and Schweitzer 1912 (score)</ref> Around the start of the [[First World War]], [[Augener & Co.|Augener]] republished [[William Thomas Best]]'s late 19th-century edition of the work in volume 2 of their complete edition of Bach's organ works.<ref>Best 1914 (score)</ref>
After 1950, when the [[Bach-Werke-Verzeichnis]] was published, it was no longer needed to indicate the Toccata and Fugue in D minor as "Peters Vol. IV, No. 4", as "[[Bach-Gesellschaft-Ausgabe|BGA]] Volume XV p. 267", as "Novello VI, 1", or without "Dorian", to distinguish it from the Toccata and Fugue with the same key signature. From then on the work has been simply BWV 565, and the other, the so-called "Dorian", has been [[BWV 538]]. In 1964, the [[New Bach Edition]] included BWV 565 in Series IV, Volume 6,<ref>Kilian 1964 (scores)</ref> with its critical commentary published in Volume 5 in 1979.<ref>Kilian 1979</ref> [[Dietrich Kilian]], the editor of these volumes, explains in the introduction to Vol. 6 that the New Bach Edition prefers to stay close to authoritative early sources for their score presentations. For BWV 565 that means staying close to the Ringk manuscript. Consequently, the name of the piece was again given in Italian as ''Toccata con Fuga'', and the piece was again written down in D Dorian (i.e. without {{flat}} at the key). However, more modern conventions were maintained with regard to using the treble clef in the upper staff and using a separate staff for the pedal.<ref name="Ringk" /><ref name="Kilian1964pVI" />
A facsimile of Ringk's manuscript was published in 2000.{{sfn|Claus|2000}} In the 21st century, the facsimile became available online,<ref name="Ringk" /> as well as various downloadable files of previously printed editions.<ref>{{IMSLP|work=Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565 (Bach, Johann Sebastian)|cname=Toccata and Fugue in D minor, BWV 565}}</ref> In 2010, [[Breitkopf & Härtel]] initiated a new edition of Bach's organ works, with BWV 565 appearing in its fourth volume.<ref name="Zehnder2011p20" />
===Performances and recordings=== [[File:Mendelssohn-Thomaskirche-1840.png|thumb|upright=1.3|Program of Mendelssohn's 1840 organ concert: BWV 565 is listed as last piece by Bach, before the "Freie Phantasie" which was an improvisation by Mendelssohn.]] The first major public performance was by Mendelssohn, on 6 August 1840, in [[Leipzig]]. The concert was very well received by the critics, among them [[Robert Schumann]], who admired the work's famous opening as an example of Bach's sense of humor.<ref>Stinson 2006, [https://archive.org/details/receptionofbachs00stin/page/55 pp. 55–60]</ref> [[Franz Liszt]] adopted the piece into his organ repertoire. He used the [[glockenspiel]] stop for the ''Prestissimo'' triplets in the opening section, and the quintadena stop for the repeated notes in bars 12–15.<ref>Stinson 2006, [https://archive.org/details/receptionofbachs00stin/page/118 p. 118]</ref>
The work was first recorded (in abridged form as "Toccata and Finale") by [[John J. McClellan]] on the [[Salt Lake Tabernacle organ]] in [[Salt Lake City]] in late August or early September 1910 by the [[Columbia Graphophone Company]], who released it in the US in 1911 on Columbia 10-inch disc A945 and in the UK on Columbia-Rena disc 1704,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/2000140449/4892-Toccata|title=Columbia matrix 4892. Toccata / J. J. McClellan – Discography of American Historical Recordings|access-date=2020-01-07|archive-date=2017-10-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171013000816/http://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/detail/2000140449/4892-Toccata|url-status=live}}</ref> which is one of the first commercial pipe organ recordings. In 1926, the organ version of BWV 565 was recorded on 78 rpm discs.<ref>Cunningham 1926 (recording)</ref> In a 1928 concert program, Schweitzer indicated BWV 565 as one of Bach's "best-known" compositions, considering it to be a youth work.<ref>Quoted in Glaus 2013, [https://books.google.com/books?id=jDwbAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA297 pp. 297–298]</ref> Schweitzer's first recording of the piece was issued in 1935.<ref>Schweitzer 1935 (recording)</ref> In 1951, he recorded the work again.<ref name="Schweitzer1951" />
In the 1950s, a recording of [[Helmut Walcha]] playing BWV 565 on organ was released.<ref name="Walcha1947">Walcha 1947 (recording)</ref> In that, and subsequent releases of Walcha's recordings of BWV 565 on [[Deutsche Grammophon]] (DG), there is an obvious evolution of the work from "one among many" organ compositions by Bach to a definite signature piece by the composer. In early [[Archiv Produktion]] releases, the list on the sleeve contained the organ compositions in the order they appeared on the recording without distinction;<ref name="Walcha1947" /> in the 1960s, BWV 565 began to be listed first;<ref>[https://archive.org/details/mbid-9490fd12-2451-4a96-9ce8-006eeb210bc5 Walcha 1964] at the [[Internet Archive]] website</ref> by the 1980s, the font size for BWV 565 was larger than that of the other compositions;<ref>[https://archive.org/details/mbid-a805ffe1-cc11-47c3-9138-1b7496684445 Walcha 1987] at the [[Internet Archive]] website</ref> and in the 1990s, Walcha's 1963 recording of the piece became the only piece by Bach included in DG's ''Classic Mania'' CD set with popular tunes by various classical composers.<ref name="Walcha1963" /> Similarly, the album sleeves of [[Marie-Claire Alain]]'s recordings of BWV 565 in the 1960s listed the piece in the same font as the other recorded works, but by the 1980s it was in a larger font.<ref>Alain (recordings)</ref> US record companies seemed faster in putting BWV 565 forward as Bach's best-known organ piece. In 1955, [[E. Power Biggs]] recorded the Toccata 14 times, played on different European organs, and Columbia issued those recordings on a single album.<ref>Biggs 1955 (recording)</ref>
[[Hans-Joachim Schulze]] describes the force of the piece on a record sleeve:<ref>Biggs 1960 (recording), liner notes</ref><blockquote>Here is elemental and unbounded power, in impatiently ascending and descending runs and rolling masses of chords, that only with difficulty abates sufficiently to give place to the logic and balance of the fugue. With the reprise of the initial Toccata, the dramatic idea reaches its culmination amidst flying scales and with an ending of great sonority.</blockquote>
Organists recording BWV 565 more than once include [[Jean Guillou]],<ref>[http://www.bach-cantatas.com/NVP/Guillou.htm Jean Guillou – Recordings] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905084634/http://www.bach-cantatas.com/NVP/Guillou.htm |date=2015-09-05 }} at bach-cantatas.com</ref> [[Lionel Rogg]]<ref>[http://www.bach-cantatas.com/NVP/Rogg-NV1.htm Lionel Rogg – Recordings] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150905223721/http://www.bach-cantatas.com/NVP/Rogg-NV1.htm |date=2015-09-05 }} at bach-cantatas.com</ref> and [[Wolfgang Rübsam]].<ref>[http://www.bach-cantatas.com/NVP/Rubsam.htm Wolfgang Rübsam – Recordings] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150927171109/http://www.bach-cantatas.com/NVP/Rubsam.htm |date=2015-09-27 }} at bach-cantatas.com</ref> Some musicians, such as [[Karl Richter (conductor)|Karl Richter]], who did not record organ performances very often, included BWV 565 in their anthologies.<ref>Richter 1964</ref> By the end of the century, hundreds of organists had recorded BWV 565.<ref>[http://www.bach-cantatas.com/NVD/Organ-Complete.htm Organ Works BWV 525–771: Recorded Sets of Bach's Complete (or near complete) Organ Works] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150822113456/http://www.bach-cantatas.com/NVD/Organ-Complete.htm |date=2015-08-22 }} at bach-cantatas.com</ref> In the 21st century, several recordings of BWV 565 became available online, such as a recording included in [[James Kibbie]]'s Bach Organ Works project and John Scott Whiteley's broadcast for BBC TV<ref>Whiteley2001</ref> made in 2001.<ref>Kibbie (recording)</ref>

===In Bach's biographies=== In [[Johann Nikolaus Forkel]]'s early 19th-century [[Johann Sebastian Bach: His Life, Art, and Work|biography of Bach]], the work is left unmentioned. Forkel probably did not even know of the composition.<ref>[[Johann Nikolaus Forkel]] (1802), translated by [[Charles Sanford Terry (historian)|Charles Sanford Terry]] (1920). [https://archive.org/details/johannsebastian01terrgoog ''Johann Sebastian Bach: His Life, Art, and Work''] New York: Harcourt, Brace and Howe; London: Constable. [https://archive.org/stream/johannsebastian01terrgoog#page/n181/mode/1up p. 134]</ref> In C. L. Hilgenfeldt's [[Biographies of Johann Sebastian Bach|biography]] it is merely listed among the published works. Hilgenfeldt considers the [[Toccata and Fugue in F major, BWV 540|Toccata and Fugue in F major]] the most accomplished of Bach's toccatas for organ.<ref>C. L. Hilgenfeldt (1850). [http://www.mdz-nbn-resolving.de/urn/resolver.pl?urn=urn:nbn:de:bvb:12-bsb10528132-5 ''Johann Sebastian Bach's Leben, Wirken und Werke: ein Beitrag zur Kunstgeschichte des achtzehnten Jahrhunderts''.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171222052953/http://www.mdz-nbn-resolving.de/urn/resolver.pl?urn=urn:nbn:de:bvb:12-bsb10528132-5 |date=2017-12-22 }} Leipzig: Friedrich Hofmeister. [https://www.digitale-sammlungen.de/de/view/bsb10528132?page=150 pp. 130–131] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305043340/http://reader.digitale-sammlungen.de/de/fs1/object/display/bsb10528132_00150.html |date=2016-03-05 }}</ref> In [[Karl Hermann Bitter]]'s 1865 Bach biography, BWV 565 is only listed in an appendix.<ref>[[Karl Hermann Bitter]] (1865). ''Johann Sebastian Bach''. Berlin: Schneider. [https://www.digitale-sammlungen.de/de/view/bsb10600016?page=504 Vol. 2, Anh. II, p. cxii] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160809010551/http://reader.digitale-sammlungen.de/de/fs1/object/display/bsb10600016_00504.html |date=2016-08-09 }}</ref>
In 1873, [[Philipp Spitta]] devoted somewhat less than a page to the work in the first volume of [[Spitta's Johann Sebastian Bach|his Bach biography]]. He assumed the work was written in the first year of Bach's second [[Weimar]] period (1708–1717). He saw more north German characteristics (Buxtehude's restless style) in the form of the Toccata, rather than south German (Pachelbel's simple and quiet approach). Spitta considered the fugue "particularly suited to the organ, and more especially effective in the pedal part." His description of the piece refers to long sections that are surfeit: "rocking passages which have no connection whatever with the chief idea" and organ recitatives alternating with "ponderous, roaring masses of chords". Spitta likened some phrases of the Toccata and Fugue to another early work, the [[Fugue in G minor, BWV 578]].<ref name="Spitta1873p402" /><ref name="Spitta1899p403" />
Spitta also detects a rhythmic figure that appears briefly in the concluding part of the work (bar 137) which, extensively elaborated, reappears in the keyboard [[Prelude in A minor, BWV 922]], a work he supposes to have been composed around 1710.<ref name="Spitta1899p434" /><ref name="Spitta1873p429">Spitta 1873, [https://books.google.com/books?id=HxkDAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA429 Vol. I pp. 429–31]</ref> In [[Reginald Lane Poole]]'s 1882 biography, the work is again merely listed.<ref>[[Reginald Lane Poole]] (1882). [https://archive.org/details/sebastianbach01poolgoog ''Sebastian Bach''.] London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle, & Rivington. [https://archive.org/stream/sebastianbach01poolgoog#page/n50/mode/1up p. 40]</ref> In the 1905 first version of his Bach biography, Albert Schweitzer leaves BWV 565 unmentioned in the chapter on the organ works.<ref>Schweitzer 1905, [https://archive.org/stream/jsbachlemusicien00schw#page/174/mode/2up pp. 174–83]</ref> In [[André Pirro]]'s 1906 biography, Bach's organ toccatas are only mentioned as a group. He considers none of them written before Bach's later Weimar years (so closer to 1717 than to 1708).<ref name="Pirro1906">[[André Pirro]] (1906). ''J.-S. Bach''. Paris: Félix Alcan. (in third edition:) [https://archive.org/stream/jsbachpi00pirr#page/216/mode/1up p. 216]; [https://archive.org/stream/jsbachpi00pirr#page/219/mode/1up pp. 219–220]</ref>
Up to this point, none of the biographers seem to have given any special attention to BWV 565. If mentioned, it is listed or described along with other organ compositions, but is far from being considered the best or the most famous of Bach's organ compositions, or even of his toccatas. However, that was about to change. In 1908, Schweitzer reworked his biography for its first German edition. In that edition he indicates the work as "well known".<ref name="Schweitzers1908">Schweitzer 1908, [https://archive.org/stream/jsbach01schwgoog#page/n276/mode/1up p. 248]</ref> After listing several organ works in which Bach showed himself a pupil of Buxtehude, Frescobaldi, and various contemporary Italian composers, Schweitzer describes the Toccata and Fugue in D minor as a work in which the composer rises to independent mastery:{{blockquote|In the D minor toccata and fugue, the strong and ardent spirit has finally realised the laws of form. A single dramatic ground-thought unites the daring passage work of the toccata, that seems to pile up like wave on wave; and in the fugue the intercalated passages in broken chords only serve to make the climax all the more powerful.<ref name="Schweitzer1935">Schweitzer 1935, [https://archive.org/stream/jsbachsc01schwuoft#page/269/mode/1up Vol. I p. 269.]</ref>}}
In [[Hubert Parry]]'s 1909 Bach biography, the work is qualified as "well known" and "one of the most effective of [Bach's] works in every way". He calls the Toccata "brilliantly rhapsodical", more or less follows Spitta in the description of the fugue, and is most impressed by the coda: "It would be hard to find a concluding passage more imposing or more absolutely adapted to the requirements of the instrument than this coda." Apart from seeing Buxtehude's influence, he likens the theme of the fugue to the theme of the fugue of [[Prelude and Fugue in B minor, BWV 544]], which he considers a late work.<ref name="Parry1909">Parry 1909, [https://archive.org/stream/johannsebastianb00parruoft#page/64/mode/2up pp. 64–65] and [https://archive.org/stream/johannsebastianb00parruoft#page/512/mode/1up p. 512]</ref>
In the 1979 first volume of his Bach biography, [[Alberto Basso]] calls BWV 565 "famosissimo" (most famous) and "celebratissima" (most celebrated), maintaining that the popularity of these works hinges entirely on this composition. He sees it as a youth work, composed before 1708, that with its underdeveloped fugue is stylistically eclectic but unified without breaking continuity. He links it to the northern school, and mentions Tausig, Busoni and Stokowki as influencing its trajectory. Basso warns against seeing too much in the composition. He feels it may be within reach of everyone but is neither an incantation, nor ridden with symbolism and even less a sum of whatever.<ref name="Basso1979">[[Alberto Basso]] (1979). ''Frau Musika: La vita e le opere di J. S. Bach'', Volume 1 (of 2): [https://books.google.com/books?id=hpiUBtwrtM4C ''Le origini familiari, l'ambiente luterano, gli anni giovanili, Weimar e Köthen (1685–1723)''.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200803212323/https://books.google.com/books?id=hpiUBtwrtM4C |date=2020-08-03 }} Turin, EDT. {{ISBN|8870630110}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=hpiUBtwrtM4C&pg=PA491 p. 491] and [https://books.google.com/books?id=hpiUBtwrtM4C&pg=PA493 pp. 493 ff.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200803220007/https://books.google.com/books?id=hpiUBtwrtM4C&pg=PA493 |date=2020-08-03 }}</ref>
In his 1999 Bach biography, {{ill|Klaus Eidam|de}} devotes a few pages to the Toccata and Fugue. He considers it an early work, probably composed for testing the technical qualities of a new organ. He feels that the crescendo that develops through arpeggios, gradually building up to the use of hundreds of pipes at the same time, can show exactly at what point the wind system of the organ might become inadequate. In his view, some of the more unusual characteristics of the piece can be explained as resulting from Bach's capacity as an organ tester.<ref name="EidamCh4">{{harvnb|Eidam|2001|loc=ch. IV}}</ref>
[[Christoph Wolff]], in his 2000 Bach biography, sees BWV 565 as an early work.<ref name="Wolff2002aP72">Wolff 2000, [https://books.google.com/books?id=YtJVFiHnepcC&pg=PA72 p. 72]</ref> In his view, it is "as refreshingly imaginative, varied, and ebullient as it is structurally undisciplined and unmastered".<ref name="Wolff2000p169">Wolff 2000 [https://books.google.com/books?id=YtJVFiHnepcC p. 169]</ref>
===In books on Bach's organ works=== Before his 1906 Bach biography, André Pirro had already written a book on Bach's organ works. In that book he devoted less than a page to BWV 565, and considers it some kind of program music depicting a tempest, including flashes of lightning and rumbling thunder. Pirro supposes Bach had success with this music in the smaller German courts he visited. All in all, he judges the music as superficial, not more than a stepping stone in Bach's development.<ref name="Pirro1902p35" /><ref>Pirro 1895, [https://archive.org/stream/lorguedejeansbas00pirr#page/66/mode/2up p. 66]</ref>
In the early 1920s, Harvey Grace published a series of articles on Bach's organ works. He considers that the notes of the piece are not too difficult to play, but that an organist performing the work is primarily challenged by interpretation. He gives tips on how to perform the work so that it does not sound like a "meaningless scramble". He describes the fugue as slender and simple, but only a "very sketchy example of the form". In his description of the piece, Grace refers to Pirro, elaborating Pirro's "storm" analogy, and like Pirro, he seems convinced Bach went touring with the piece. His suggestions for the organ registration make comparisons with how the piece would be played by an orchestra.<ref name="Grace1922p60" />
In 1948, [[Hermann Keller]] wrote that the Toccata and Fugue was uncharacteristic for Bach, but nonetheless bore some of his distinguishing marks.<ref>Emans 2004, [https://books.google.com/books?id=DG7t3TgLKyAC&pg=PA26 p. 26]</ref> His description of the piece echoes earlier storm analogies. Keller sees the opening bars' unison passages as "descending like a lightning flash, the long roll of thunder of the broken chords of the full organ, and the stormy undulation of the triplets".<ref name="Keller1948p64" />
In 1980, [[Peter Williams (Musicologist)|Peter Williams]] wrote about BWV 565 in the first volume of his ''The Organ Music of J.S.Bach''. The author warns against numerological over-interpretation like that of Volker Gwinner. Many parts of the composition are described as typical of Bach. Williams sees stylistic matches with Pachelbel, with the north German organ school, and with the Italian violin school, but sees various unusual features of the composition as well. Williams questions the authenticity of the piece, based on its various unusual features, and elaborates the idea that the piece may have a violin version ancestor.<ref name="Williams1980p215">Williams 1980, [https://books.google.com/books?id=JfE6AAAAIAAJ&pg=PA214 pp. 214–221]</ref> The reworked edition of this book, in one volume, appeared in 2003, and devotes more pages to discussing the authenticity and possible prior versions of BWV 565. In the meantime, Williams had written a 1981 article on the authenticity of BWV 565; this was followed by numerous publications by other scholars on the same topic.{{sfn|Williams|2003}}<ref>Gwinner 1968</ref>
''J. S. Bach as Organist'', a 1986 collection of essays edited by George Stauffer and Ernest May, discussed the registration Bach would have used for BWV 565.<ref>Stauffer, George B. "Bach's Organ Registration Reconsidered", pp. 193–211, in {{harvnb|Stauffer|May|1986}}</ref>

[[Oskar Fischinger]] had previously used Bach's [[Brandenburg concerto no. 3|Third Brandenburg Concerto]] to accompany abstract animations and suggested to Stokowski that his orchestral version of BWV 565 could be used in the same way. Later in 1937, while in [[California]], Stokowski and [[Walt Disney|Disney]] discussed the idea of making a short animated film of ''[[The Sorcerer's Apprentice (Dukas)|The Sorcerer's Apprentice]]'' by [[Paul Dukas|Dukas]] for [[Walt Disney Productions|Disney Studios]], the intention being to introduce classical music to a younger and broader audience. Similar in spirit to the popular series of ''[[Silly Symphonies]],'' the short film proved costly to produce. However, starting with the Toccata and Fugue and the Sorcerer's Apprentice, Stokowski, Disney and the music critic [[Deems Taylor]] chose other compositions to incorporate into their film project, known as "The Concert Feature". By the time Disney's ''[[Fantasia (1940 film)|Fantasia]]'' was released in 1940, the animations accompanying BWV 565 had been made semi-abstract, although Fischinger's original idea that the performance of the music start with showing Stokowski directing his orchestra was preserved. Taylor begins his narrative with, "What you’re going to see is the designs and pictures and stories of what music inspired in the minds and imaginations of a group of artists." The opening number, the "Toccata and Fugue," will be [[absolute music]]—music that exists for its own sake—and will try to depict what might go on in the mind of the person listening to it. "At first you are more or less conscious of the orchestra," Taylor explains, "so our picture opens with a series of impressions of the conductor and the players. Then the music begins to suggest other things to your imagination—oh, just masses of color, or cloud forms, or vague shadows, or geometrical objects floating in space." In the 1942 cinema release of the film by RKO, the Toccata and Fugue was cut entirely, only to return in a 1946 re-release. ''Fantasia'' contributed significantly to the popularity of the Toccata and Fugue.<ref name="Zehnder2012">{{cite book|url=https://www.breitkopf.com/assets/pdf/15014_EB8804_PDF_EB8804_Einl.pdf|title=Bach's Complete Organ Works, Volume 4|chapter=Introduction|first=Jean-Claude|last=Zehnder|author-link=Jean-Claude Zehnder|publisher=[[Breitkopf & Härtel]]|year=2012|location=Wiesbaden|pages=16–24|access-date=2020-11-05|archive-date=2015-09-10|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150910224148/https://www.breitkopf.com/assets/pdf/15014_EB8804_PDF_EB8804_Einl.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Farmer2000p192">{{cite book|first=Clark|last= Farmer|year= 2008| chapter="Every Beautiful Sound Also Creates an Equally Beautiful Picture": Color Music and Walt Disney's Fantasia|pages= 183–97|title=Lowering the Boom: Critical Studies in Film Sound|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VoKROBFWuvoC| editor1= Jay Beck| editor2= Tony Grajeda|publisher= [[University of Illinois Press]]| isbn=978-0252075322}} [https://books.google.com/books?id=VoKROBFWuvoC&pg=PA192 See pp. 192–97]</ref><ref name="Mickey1">{{cite book|first=Michael|last=Barrier|title=The Animated Man: A Life of Walt Disney|series=Simpson Book in the Humanities|publisher=[[University of California Press]]|year= 2007|isbn= 978-0520941663}}</ref><ref name="Mickey2">{{cite book |title=Reinventing Bach|first=Paul|last= Elie|publisher=Aurum Press|year= 2013|isbn= 978-1908526410}}</ref><ref name="Mickey3">{{cite book|title=America's Film Legacy: The Authoritative Guide to the Landmark Movies in the National Film Registry|first=Daniel| last=Eagan|publisher=A&C Black|year= 2010|isbn=978-0826429773|pages=323–24}}</ref>

===Authenticity research and reconstructions=== A certain uneasiness regarding the authorship of BWV 565 had been around long before the 1980s. From Hilgenfeldt in 1850, to Elgar in the 1920s, to Basso in the late 1970s, the extraordinary popularity of the piece seems to have taken scholars and musicians by surprise. Mendelssohn felt it was something for both the erudite and the masses. Some scholars who analysed the composition's counterpoint felt it was substandard.<ref name="Grace1922p60" /><ref name="Williams1980p215" /><ref name="Davies1961">Davies, Antony (1961). "New light on Bach" in ''[[Musical Opinion]]'' Vol. 84, pp. 755–759</ref><ref name="Bullivant1971p14">{{harvnb|Bullivant|1971|p=14}} and elsewhere</ref> They said it was stylistically too close to the [[galant music|galant style]] of the later 18th century to be an early 18th-century composition.<ref name="Zehnder2011p20" /> Its presumed time of composition shifted around. Some felt the composition was too modern to have been composed by a young Bach,<ref name="Pirro1906" /><ref name="Williams1980p215" /> or too simplistic to have been composed by a middle-aged Bach.<ref name="Basso1979" /><ref name="Bullivant1971p14" /> Although many commentators have invoked Bach's genius to explain the dislocated modernity in an immature composition,<ref name="Fagius1988liner" /><ref name="Keller1948p64" /><ref name="EidamCh4" /> an increasing number of scholars felt unsatisfied with such an intangible explanation.<ref name="Williams1981" />
In a 1981 article, Peter Williams reiterated the speculations, from which he saw a way out of the conundrum, already featured in his 1980 book on Bach's organ compositions:<ref name="Williams1981" /> * The piece was originally composed for violin, not necessarily by Bach (that would explain its "simplicity"); * It was later transcribed for the organ, not necessarily by Bach (that would explain its "modernity").
The analysis of the material sources for the piece, its oldest surviving manuscripts, although insufficiently pursued according to some scholars,<ref name="Emans2009p103">Emans 2009, [https://books.google.com/books?id=G78Fu6PnXl8C&pg=PA103 pp. 103 ff.]</ref> was seen as too limited to give a conclusive answer to these questions. What was available from that branch of the research could be explained in opposite ways.<ref name="Emans2009p109">Emans 2009, [https://books.google.com/books?id=G78Fu6PnXl8C&pg=PA109 p. 109]</ref> Likewise, whether the more elaborate stylistic evidence was considered conclusive or merely circumstantial, depended on who was trying to prove what.<ref name="Zehnder2011p20" />
In 1982, David Humphreys suggested that BWV 565 may have been composed and/or arranged by Kellner, or by someone from the circle around Kellner.<ref name="Williams1981" /><ref>Humphreys 1982, pp. 216–217</ref> Despite many stylistic similarities,<ref>Stephan Emele (2000). [http://www.johann-peter-kellner.de/index.php?sub=werke&page=bwv565 4.6 "BWV 565 – ein Werk von Kellner?"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304001518/http://www.johann-peter-kellner.de/index.php?sub=werke&page=bwv565 |date=2016-03-04 }} in ''Ein Beispiel der mitteldeutschen Orgelkunst des 18. Jahrhunderts: Johann Peter Kellner'' (thesis). Jena. {{OCLC|553465573}}</ref> however, Kellner was ruled out a quarter of a century later: "in comparison with the style of Kellner, BWV 565 more resembles the style of J. S. Bach";<ref name="KranenburgII">Kranenburg 2007/2008</ref> "many of Kellner's keyboard pieces revealed that his style boasts pronounced ''galant'' elements ... this clearly stands in strong contrast to the dramatic style of the Toccata BWV 565".<ref name="Zehnder2011p20" />
A violin composition by Bach's eldest son [[Wilhelm Friedemann Bach|Wilhelm Friedemann]], transcribed for the organ by Ringk, was named as another possible source.<ref name="Fagius1988liner" /> However, according to 21st-century [[statistical analysis]], Wilhelm Friedemann was even less likely to have been the composer of the Fugue than Kellner.<ref name="KranenburgII" /> The same research indicated that large portions of the Fugue were consistent with the style of [[Johann Ludwig Krebs]], but with more than half of the Fugue more likely composed by J. S. Bach.<ref name="KranenburgII" /> After initially confirming Williams's doubts about the authorship of BWV 565,<ref name="Kranenburg2006">Kranenburg 2006</ref> by the second decade of the 21st century, statistical analysis left the attribution issue undecided. No-one had found a composer more compatible with the style of its fugue than Bach himself.<ref name="Kranenburg2010" /> In the words of [[Jean-Claude Zehnder]], who was sympathetic towards the violin version reconstruction: "The matter still remains open, despite the scholarly discourse that began in 1981. Until proof of the contrary, BWV 565 should be considered as a work by Johann Sebastian Bach."<ref name="Zehnder2011p20" /> No edition of the [[Bach Werke Verzeichnis]] has listed BWV 565 among the works seen as spurious or doubtful,<ref>[[Alfred Dürr|Dürr, Alfred]]; Kobayashi, Yoshitake; Beißwenger, Kirsten (1998). ''[[Bach Werke Verzeichnis]]'' (version 2a). Wiesbaden: [[Breitkopf & Härtel]]. {{ISBN|3765102490}} [http://bachmidi.info/kbwv-07.html#p0324 p. 324] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160123065516/http://bachmidi.info/kbwv-07.html#p0324 |date=2016-01-23 }}</ref> nor does the work's entry on the website of the [[Bach Archiv Leipzig]] mention any doubts.<ref>[http://www.bach-digital.de/receive/BachDigitalWork_work_00000645 Toccata in d BWV 565] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304050026/http://www.bach-digital.de/receive/BachDigitalWork_work_00000645 |date=2016-03-04 }} at {{URL|www.bach-digital.de}}</ref>
====Attribution question==== In 1961, Antony Davies remarked that the Toccata was void of counterpoint.<ref name="Davies1961" /> Half a decade later, BWV 565 was further questioned. Walter Emery advocated that scepticism was a necessary condition to approaching the history of Bach's organ compositions,<ref name="Emery1966">Emery 1966</ref> and [[Friedrich Blume]] saw problems with the traditional historiography of Bach's youth.{{sfn|Blume|1968}} Roger Bullivant thought the fugue too simple for Bach and saw characteristics that were incompatible with his style:<ref name="Bullivant1971p14" /> * Conclusion of the piece on a minor plagal cadence * A pedal statement of the subject, unaccompanied by other voices * Trill in bars 86 to 90 These doubts about the authorship of BWV 565 were elaborated by Peter Williams in a 1981 article. Hypotheses proposed by Williams in that article included that BWV 565 may have been composed after 1750 and may have been based on an earlier composition for another instrument, supposedly violin. Williams added more stylistic problems to the ones already mentioned by Bullivant, among others the [[parallel octaves]] throughout the opening of the toccata, the true subdominant answers in the fugue, and the primitive harmonies throughout the piece, with countersubjects in the fugue frequently moving through thirds and sixths only. All of these characteristics are either unique or extremely rare in organ music of the first half of the 18th century.<ref name="Williams1981" />
In 1995, Rolf Dietrich Claus decided against the authenticity of BWV 565, mainly based on the stylistic characteristics of the piece.<ref name="Emans2009p103" /> He named another problem—in its first measure the composition contains a C{{sharp}}, a note organs in Bach's time rarely had, and which Bach almost never used in his organ compositions.{{sfn|Billeter|2004}} In his book on BWV 565, which he expanded in 1998 to counter some of the criticisms it received, Claus also dismisses the prior-version options suggested by Williams, noting that the toccata was an unknown genre for violin solo compositions of the time.<ref>Claus 1998</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Claus|2018}}</ref> Several essays in [[John Butt (musician)|John Butt]]'s [[List of Cambridge Companions to Music|Cambridge Companion]] on Bach discuss the attribution problems of BWV 565.<ref>Butt 1997, [https://books.google.com/books?id=YiJKHGxrYzsC&pg=PA76 p. 76] and elsewhere.</ref> Other biographers and scholars have left these attribution and prior-version theories unmentioned,<ref name="EidamCh4" /> or explained the atypical characteristics of the composition by indicating it was a very early composition by Bach, probably written during his stay in [[Arnstadt]] (1703–1706).<ref name="Wolff2002aP72" />
At the end of the 20th century, [[Hans Fagius]] wrote:{{blockquote|... the fact remains that the Toccata is strikingly unorganistic and modern to have been written by Bach around 1705, even if the form is that of North German toccata. There are, however, few organ pieces with so much spirit and drive, and why should not a genius like Bach, in youthful high spirits, have produced this unique work, which is in some respects half a century before its time and which could achieve a place as one of the most beloved compositions in all of music history?<ref name="Fagius1988liner" />}}
The authorship debate has continued in the 21st century. Wolff calls it a pseudo-problem.<ref>Wolf 2002</ref> Williams suggested that the piece may have been created by another composer who must have been born in the beginning of the 18th century, since details of style (such as triadic harmony, spread chords, and the use of solo pedal) may indicate post-1730, or even post-1750 idioms.{{sfn|Williams|2003}} Statistical analysis conducted by Peter van Kranenburg in 2006 confirmed the fugue was atypical for Bach,<ref name="Kranenburg2006" /> but failed to find a composer more likely to have composed it than Bach.<ref name="Kranenburg2010" /> David Schulenberg feels that the attribution of BWV 565 to Bach is doubtful.<ref>Schulenberg 2006, [https://books.google.com/books?id=GnbGQzhz0SgC&pg=PA434 p. 434], [https://books.google.com/books?id=GnbGQzhz0SgC&pg=PA458 p. 458] and [https://books.google.com/books?id=GnbGQzhz0SgC&pg=PA516 p. 516]</ref> [[Richard D. P. Jones|Richard Douglas Jones]] takes no position with regard to the composition's authenticity.<ref>Jones 2007 p. 160</ref> In 2009, Reinmar Emans wrote that Claus and Wolff had diametrically opposed views on the reliability of Ringk as a copyist, inspired by their respective positions in the authenticity debate, and thinks that sort of speculation unhelpful.<ref name="Emans2009p109"/>
====Anterior version hypothesis and reconstructions==== [[File:BachToccataAndFugueInDMinorOpeningViolinVersion.GIF|thumb|upright=1.3|Transposed to A minor and adapted for the violin, the opening offers an opportunity to drop down through all four strings of the instrument.<ref name="Williams1981p336">Williams 1981, p. 336</ref>]] [[File:BachToccataAndFugueInDMinorRecastAsViolinMusic.PNG|thumb|upright=1.3|Quadruple stops, not uncommon for 18th-century solo violin music, could have been used in passages such as this, taken from the ending.]] The other hypothesis elaborated by Williams is that BWV 565 may have been a transcription of a lost solo violin piece. Parallel octaves and the preponderance of thirds and sixths may be explained by a transcriber's attempt to fill in harmony which, if preserved as is, would be inadequately thin on a pipe organ. This is corroborated by the fact that the subject of the fugue, and certain passages (such as bars 12–15), are evidently inspired by string music. Bach is known to have transcribed solo violin works for organ at least twice: the first movement of the [[Partita for Violin No. 3 (Bach)|Partita in E major for solo violin]], BWV 1006, was converted by Bach into the solo organ part of the opening movement of the cantata [[Wir danken dir, Gott, wir danken dir, BWV 29|''Wir danken dir, Gott, wir danken dir'', BWV 29]]. Bach also transcribed the Fugue movement of Sonata in G minor for solo violin, [[BWV 1001]], as the second half of Prelude and Fugue in D minor for organ, [[List of compositions by Johann Sebastian Bach#BWV531|BWV 539]].
This notion inspired a new theory of adaptation: the reconstruction. Reconstructions have been applied to several other works by Bach, with variable success.<ref>[[Peter Wollny]], [http://www.eclassical.com/shop/17115/art33/4951433-c30ca2-3149020218129_01.pdf "Harpsichord Concertos" pp. 6–7] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150922030721/http://www.eclassical.com/shop/17115/art33/4951433-c30ca2-3149020218129_01.pdf |date=2015-09-22 }} in booklet notes for [[Andreas Staier]]'s 2015 recording of the concertos, Harmonia mundi HMC 902181.82</ref> A reconstruction for violin has been played by [[Jaap Schröder]]<ref name="Williams1981p337">Williams 1981, p. 337</ref> and [[Simon Standage]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Rockwell |first=John |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9C06E6D71038F930A2575AC0A962948260 |title=Concert: Academy of Ancient Music |journal=[[New York Times]] |date=September 13, 1984 |access-date=2011-09-29 |archive-date=2009-02-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090220090442/http://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9C06E6D71038F930A2575AC0A962948260 |url-status=live }}</ref> The violinist [[Andrew Manze]] produced his own reconstruction, also in A minor, which he has performed and recorded.<ref>''Johann Sebastian Bach / Andrew Manze, Richard Egarr, Jaap ter Linden – Four Violin Sonatas; Toccata and Fugue, BWV 565''. BBC MM89, 1999.</ref> In 2000, Mark Argent proposed a [[scordatura]] five-stringed cello instead.<ref name="Argent2000" /> Williams proposed a [[cello da spalla|violoncello piccolo]] or a five-stringed cello as alternative possibilities in 2003.{{sfn|Williams|2003}} A new violin version was created by scholar Bruce Fox-Lefriche in 2004.<ref>Fox-Lefriche 2004</ref> In 2005, Eric Lewin Altschuler wrote that if the first version of BWV 565 was written for a stringed instrument the most likely candidate would have been a [[lute]].{{sfn|Altschuler|2005}} Yet another violin version was created by Chad Kelly and performed by [[Rachel Podger]] on her 2022 album ''Tutta Sola''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.prestomusic.com/classical/articles/5003--interview-rachel-podger-on-tutta-sola|title=Rachel Podger on Tutta Sola|publisher=Presto Music|date=22 November 2022|access-date=11 February 2024}}</ref>
In 1997, Bernhard Billeter proposed a [[harpsichord]] toccata original,{{sfn|Billeter|2004}} which was deemed unlikely by Williams.{{sfn|Williams|2003}} However, Billeter's argument makes authorship by Bach more likely: Bach's [[Toccatas for Keyboard (Bach)|harpsichord toccatas]] (most of them early works) have simplistic elements and quirks similar to BWV 565.{{sfn|Billeter|2004}} Bach's early keyboard works, especially the free ones like Preludes and Toccatas, cannot always be clearly separated into organ pieces and harpsichord pieces. Spitta had already remarked on the similarity between a passage in BWV 565 and one in the harpsichord Prelude BWV 921; Robert Marshall compares the continuation patterns and sequences of the harpsichord Toccata [[BWV 911]], and the Fugue theme of the harpsichord Toccata [[BWV 914]], with the same of BWV 565.<ref name="Marshall2003" /><ref name="Spitta1899p434" />
===In literature=== In 1935, [[Hermann Hesse]] wrote a poem about the piece, {{lang|de|Zu einer Toccata von Bach}} ("On a toccata by Bach"), which contributed to its fame.<ref name="Zehnder2011p20" /><ref>[http://www.deutschelyrik.de/index.php/zu-einer-toccata-von-bach.html "Zu einer Toccata von Bach"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304071504/http://www.deutschelyrik.de/index.php/zu-einer-toccata-von-bach.html |date=2016-03-04 }} at {{URL|www.deutschelyrik.de}}</ref>
